> > Mike,
> >
> > Thank you very much for your response; this is very helpful information. Just to clarify further, is it not advisable to try to use any microclimate model to predict air temperatures just above (e.g., 5 cm) the surface of a body of water? We are primarily concerned with estimating fine-scale air temperatures and would like to know if we can incorporate characteristics of the radiative/reflective environment that characterizes a body of water in the microclimate modeling setting to do this. Otherwise we will definitely look into the general lake model for our purposes.
> >
> > Thank you so much for your help and advice.
> >
> > Best regards,
> >
> > Joseph
> >
> > On Tue, Sep 19, 2023 at 2:28 AM NicheMapR <nich...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Joseph,
> > >
> > > The microclimate model approach of simulating a clay pan can give you a good estimate of wetland depth, and the 'bucket model' approach in the ectotherm model will predict the 'core temperature' of the bucket, but neither are really meant for predicting microclimates at the surface of a water body. It really is a job for a hydrological model like the general lake model <https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/12/473/2019/gmd-12-473-2019.html>. The endotherm model can be used to simulate a duck's energetics when sitting on the surface or diving. There are some good papers on this by Warren Porter and colleagues on seabirds <https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/212/15/2483/18443/Thermodynamic-modelling-predicts-energetic>. It is specific about the dorsal and ventral environment and you can also change the 'fluid' to water.
> > >
> > > Note that whatever you do the predictions will be computationally expensive and you might get just as much of an understanding by some judicious point analyses rather than generating (admittedly less satisfying) gridded outputs. At least it is worth exploring and carefully testing how well you can make predictions using points first.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps.
> > >
> > > All the best,
> > > Mike

> > > On Tuesday, September 19, 2023 at 7:26:57 AM UTC+10 josephm...@gmail.com wrote:

> > > >
> > > > I am an MS student working on a research project where a key step is to produce gridded hourly rasters of microclimate air temperatures at the surface of wetlands and adjacent upland areas. I plan to use the ERA5 hourly reanalysis and various terrain/vegetation data as inputs. The NicheMapR-microclima workflow seems appropriate to produce gridded outputs at the resolution I need.  I’ve reviewed the posts and relevant papers where the clay rainfall catchment method to simulate pond temperatures was used, but these seem to be mostly for partially-to fully-submerged ectotherms. My aim is use this for a semi-aquatic endotherm that spends most of its time feeding or loafing on the surface of the water (dabbling duck). I am inquiring if this method also is applicable for simulating air temperature at the surface of bodies of water? If so, can it be readily integrated into the NicheMapR-microclima gridded output workflow?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thank you for your time and consideration. Please let me know if you have any additional questions regarding the information and inquiry provided.
> > > >

messages.subject: Re: The location parameters....
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,
No it will just calculate the heat and water exchange based on the translation into microclimate of whatever the climate and terrain/soil properties you use. You could account for the specific properties of a road and try to predict road temperature compared to adjacent soil, but that would be through how you set up the thermal properties of the 'soil' in the microclimate model. In essence, these models can tell you the potential body temperatures and water loss rates your animal might have in a given location, which you can then use to understand what microclimates it might be selecting (shade, going underground, climbing) and how this would affect its survival, growth and reproduction. For a general intro, have a read of this paper <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/gcb.16557>.
All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: clear sky radiation vs real solar radiation
messages.subject_clean: clear sky radiation vs real solar radiation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Liang,

You could set TAI to zero. But, if you really want to know what the radiation would be without the effects of the atmosphere, other than the permanent gases in the atmosphere that scatter radiation (a 'Rayleigh atmosphere') you could integrate the outputs from the drrlam table that are produced if you set 'lam = 1'. E.g. here's a plot of the Rayleigh vs the direct and scattered radiation at midday on the 15th Jan for the default location (Madison, Wisconsin):

library(NicheMapR)
micro <- micro_global(lamb = 1, IUV = 1, timeinterval = 12)
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
drlam <- as.data.frame(micro$drlam) # direct solar
drrlam <- as.data.frame(micro$drrlam) # Rayleigh solar
srlam <- as.data.frame(micro$srlam) # scattered solar
lambda <- as.numeric(colnames(drlam)[3:113]) # get the wavelengths
plot(lambda, drrlam[13, 3:113], type = 'l', col = 1, ylab = 'W/m2/nm', xlab = 'wave length, nm')
points(lambda, drlam[13, 3:113], type = 'l', col = 2)
points(lambda, srlam[13, 3:113], type = 'l', col = 3)

Black is the Rayleigh atmosphere, and then you can see the effect of water/aerosols/ozone in the red line.

Here's what you get if you just set the aerosols to zero (TAI = rep(0, 111)):

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: era5 download issues
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I haven't had a successful download of era5 in recent months. It always froze at:
 User XXX for cds service added successfully in keychain file
[1] "Downloading: -180_-175_2022.nc <http://180_-175_2022.nc>" Requesting data to the cds service with username 117622 - staging data transfer at url endpoint or request id:  6f8a6161-beea-4004-bfc9-44426d35ca2c - timeout set to 5.0 hours

My ecmwfr version was 1.5.0.

The code I used for downloading is:
    req<-build_era5_request(xmin = xmn, xmax = xmx,
                            ymin = ymn, ymax = ymx,
                            start_time = st_time,
                            end_time = en_time,
                            outfile_name = file_prefix)
    request_era5(request = req, uid = uid1, out_path = op)

Any suggestions? Your help would be most appreciated!

Liang

On Wednesday, November 9, 2022 at 10:44:57 AM UTC+8 dkli...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi André,
>
> If by model you mean the NicheMapR microclimate model, yes most of the NicheMapR wrapper functions that leverage the microclimate model have some option to save downloaded climate and re-access the local data, or you can modify one of the wrapper functions to access a custom climate dataset (from experience this may take a bit of effort). However I want to note that for all of the NicheMapR wrapper functions– including micro_era5 that uses mcera5– once you download the climate dataset once, if you set save = 1 then the climate forcing data will be saved (setting save = 2 will access saved climate data). For downloading ERA5 data via mcera5, I want to note that the download times are mostly due to the CDS API server, which is out of control of mcera5 and will be the case no matter what fashion you download CDS data. But, once downloaded, you won't need to do so again for the same time and place.
>
> Best,
> Dave
> ᐧ

Hi Liang,

Sorry to hear that you've had troubles. Could you send me the input values for build_era5_request() that you attempted to use? It seems from the name of your requested file ("-180_-175_2022.nc <https://streaklinks.com/Bt4HIMop6VUxsqjKaQ5OEfKJ/http%3A%2F%2F180_-175_2022.nc>") that you have xmn = -180, xmx = -175, and some part or all of year 2022, but the function also requires ymn and ymax.

If you could send:
xmn
xmx
ymn
ymx
st_time
en_time

I'll try to reproduce your download attempt.

Best,
Dave
ᐧ
